title: Combinatorial Algorithm for Optimal Colouring of Perfect Graphs
statement_text: Construct a ``combinatorial'' polynomial-time algorithm that yields an optimal colouring of a perfect graph.
context_text: Grötschel, Lovász, and Schrijver [9] showed in 1988 that the ellipsoid method finds an $\omega(G)$-colouring of any perfect graph in polynomial time. Finding a combinatorial algorithm achieving the same has remained a well-known open question in the field ever since.
paper_contribution: Gives a combinatorial algorithm (Algorithm 1.1) that, with input an $n$-vertex Berge graph, outputs an optimal colouring in time $O(n^{(\omega(G)+1)^2})$, which is polynomial for fixed clique number $k = \omega(G)$.
notes: Described in the paper as a 'well-known open question' with no explicit citation to an originating author; it arises naturally from the Grötschel–Lovász–Schrijver [9] result. PDF source.
paper_title: Colouring perfect graphs with bounded clique number

title: Open Question on Number of Tight Skew Partitions
statement_text: We do not know how many tight skew partitions an $n$-vertex graph can really have; the authors do not know of a graph with more than linearly many tight skew partitions.
context_text: A skew partition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B)$ of $V(G)$ such that $G[A]$ is not connected and the complement $\overline{G}[B]$ is not connected. An anticomponent of $G[B]$ is a component of its complement. A skew partition $(A,B)$ is loose if some vertex of $A$ is adjacent to every vertex of some anticomponent of $G[B]$, or some vertex of $B$ has no neighbour in some component of $G[A]$; it is tight otherwise. Skew partitions are central in the structure theory of Berge (perfect) graphs, and the paper uses them to obtain a combinatorial algorithm that optimally colours perfect graphs with clique number $k$ in time polynomial for fixed $k$. Modifying the Kennedy–Reed algorithm, the authors list all tight skew partitions of any $n$-vertex graph in time $O(n^6)$, which shows there are at most $n^4$ of them; they improve this to at most $n^3\log n$, because for every tight skew partition $(A,B)$ the set $B$ appears at least $k_2$ times in the Kennedy–Reed list, where $k_2$ is the size of the second largest anticomponent of $G[B]$. In contrast, loose skew partitions can be exponentially many (e.g. in the star $K_{1,n}$). The true maximum number of tight skew partitions is unknown.
notes: Stated as prose without a labelled theorem environment. PDF source.
